A population of bacteria is modeled by \(P(t)=1000(2)^{t/3}\), where \(t\) is in hours. Interpret the meaning of the exponent's structure, and find the population after 9 hours.
questions.answer: The form \(2^{t/3}\) means the population doubles every 3 hours. After 9 hours (3 doubling periods): \(P(9)=1000(2)^{3}=1000(8)=8000\) bacteria.

questions.q: The graph shows \(f(x)=2^x\) and \(g(x)=3(0.5)^x\), one growing and one decaying.
parts: Identify which curve represents growth and which represents decay.
State the horizontal asymptote shared by both curves.
answers: \(f(x)=2^x\) is the growth curve (increasing, base \(>1\)). \(g(x)=3(0.5)^x\) is the decay curve (decreasing, base \(<1\)).
Both curves approach the horizontal asymptote \(y=0\) (neither ever reaches or crosses it).
questions.answer: (a) \(f(x)=2^x\) is the growth curve (increasing, base \(>1\)). \(g(x)=3(0.5)^x\) is the decay curve (decreasing, base \(<1\)).; (b) Both curves approach the horizontal asymptote \(y=0\) (neither ever reaches or crosses it).
questions.explanation: (a) \(f(x)=2^x\) is the growth curve (increasing, base \(>1\)). \(g(x)=3(0.5)^x\) is the decay curve (decreasing, base \(<1\)).; (b) Both curves approach the horizontal asymptote \(y=0\) (neither ever reaches or crosses it).

questions.q: Explain the difference between the discrete growth model \(A(t)=A_0(1+r)^t\) and the continuous growth model \(A(t)=A_0e^{kt}\), and state how \(r\) and \(k\) are related when both models describe the same annual growth rate \(r\).
questions.target: Continuous growth and the number e
questions.answer: The discrete model compounds growth once per period (e.g. once a year), while the continuous model compounds growth constantly at every instant. They're related by \(e^k=1+r\), i.e. \(k=\ln(1+r)\) — the continuous rate \(k\) is slightly less than the discrete rate \(r\) for positive growth, since continuous compounding reaches the same total growth with a slightly lower nominal rate.
questions.explanation: The discrete model compounds growth once per period (e.g. once a year), while the continuous model compounds growth constantly at every instant. They're related by \(e^k=1+r\), i.e. \(k=\ln(1+r)\) — the continuous rate \(k\) is slightly less than the discrete rate \(r\) for positive growth, since continuous compounding reaches the same total growth with a slightly lower nominal rate.

questions.q: Find the horizontal asymptote and \(y\)-intercept of \(h(x)=-3(2)^x+6\).
questions.answer: The negative coefficient reflects the graph over the horizontal asymptote line; as \(x\rightarrow\infty\), \(-3(2)^x\rightarrow-\infty\), so \(h(x)\rightarrow-\infty\), while as \(x\rightarrow-\infty\), \(-3(2)^x\rightarrow0\), giving horizontal asymptote \(y=6\). \(y\)-intercept: \(h(0)=-3(1)+6=3\), so \((0,3)\).
questions.explanation: The negative coefficient reflects the graph over the horizontal asymptote line; as \(x\rightarrow\infty\), \(-3(2)^x\rightarrow-\infty\), so \(h(x)\rightarrow-\infty\), while as \(x\rightarrow-\infty\), \(-3(2)^x\rightarrow0\), giving horizontal asymptote \(y=6\). \(y\)-intercept: \(h(0)=-3(1)+6=3\), so \((0,3)\).

questions.q: A savings account earns 4% annual interest compounded quarterly, modeled by \(A(t)=A_0\left(1+\frac{0.04}{4}\right)^{4t}\). If 5000 dollars is deposited, find the balance after 3 years, to the nearest dollar.

Explain, without computing exact values, why compounding more frequently (e.g. daily instead of quarterly) at the same nominal annual rate produces a slightly larger balance after the same number of years.
questions.answer: More frequent compounding applies the (smaller) periodic interest rate more often, and interest starts earning interest sooner and more often within each year. This pushes the effective annual growth rate slightly above the nominal rate, so daily compounding yields a marginally larger balance than quarterly compounding at the same stated annual rate.
questions.explanation: More frequent compounding applies the (smaller) periodic interest rate more often, and interest starts earning interest sooner and more often within each year. This pushes the effective annual growth rate slightly above the nominal rate, so daily compounding yields a marginally larger balance than quarterly compounding at the same stated annual rate.

questions.q: \(f(x)=-2x^2-5x+4\). Find the average rate of change of \(f\) on \([-2,-1]\).

A Ferris wheel has a diameter of \(40\mathrm{\ meters}\) and its lowest point is \(4\mathrm{\ meters}\) above the ground. Passengers board at the lowest point at \(t = 0\), and the wheel completes one full revolution every \(8\mathrm{\ minutes}\). Write a cosine model \(h(t)\) for a passenger's height at time \(t\), and find the times during the first revolution when \(h(t) = 34\mathrm{\ meters}\).
questions.answer: Step 1: Determine sinusoidal parameters: Radius (amplitude) \(= 20\mathrm{\ m}\); midline \(D = 4 + 20 = 24\mathrm{\ m}\); angular frequency \(B = \frac{2\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{4}\). Starting at the minimum gives a negative cosine: \(\mathbf{h(t) = -20\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}t\right) + 24}.\) Step 2: Solve \(h(t) = 34\) on \([0, 8]\): \(-20\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}t\right) + 24 = 34 \Rightarrow \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}t\right) = -\frac{1}{2}.\) \(\frac{\pi}{4}t = \frac{2\pi}{3}, \frac{4\pi}{3} \Rightarrow \mathbf{t = \frac{8}{3}\mathrm{\ min} \quad\mathrm{and}\quad t = \frac{16}{3}\mathrm{\ min}}.\)
questions.explanation: Step 1: Determine sinusoidal parameters: Radius (amplitude) \(= 20\mathrm{\ m}\); midline \(D = 4 + 20 = 24\mathrm{\ m}\); angular frequency \(B = \frac{2\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{4}\). Starting at the minimum gives a negative cosine: \(\mathbf{h(t) = -20\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}t\right) + 24}.\) Step 2: Solve \(h(t) = 34\) on \([0, 8]\): \(-20\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}t\right) + 24 = 34 \Rightarrow \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}t\right) = -\frac{1}{2}.\) \(\frac{\pi}{4}t = \frac{2\pi}{3}, \frac{4\pi}{3} \Rightarrow \mathbf{t = \frac{8}{3}\mathrm{\ min} \quad\mathrm{and}\quad t = \frac{16}{3}\mathrm{\ min}}.\)

questions.q: The half-life of Carbon-14 is 5730 years. (a) Write \(A(t)\). (b) How much of 200 g remains after 11 460 years? (c) When is only 10% left?
questions.answer: (a) Exponential Decay Function: \(A(t) = 200\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/5730}.\) (b) Mass Remaining at \(t = 11{,}460\) years: Notice that \(\frac{11{,}460}{5730} = 2\) half-lives: \(A(11{,}460) = 200\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = 200\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) = \mathbf{50\mathrm{\ g}}.\) (c) Time to Reach 10% of Initial Mass: Set \(\frac{A(t)}{200} = 0.10\): \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/5730} = 0.10 \Rightarrow \frac{t}{5730}\ln(0.5) = \ln(0.10) \Rightarrow t = 5730\frac{\ln(0.10)}{\ln(0.5)} \approx \mathbf{19{,}035\mathrm{\ years}}.\)
questions.explanation: (a) Exponential Decay Function: \(A(t) = 200\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/5730}.\) (b) Mass Remaining at \(t = 11{,}460\) years: Notice that \(\frac{11{,}460}{5730} = 2\) half-lives: \(A(11{,}460) = 200\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = 200\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) = \mathbf{50\mathrm{\ g}}.\) (c) Time to Reach 10% of Initial Mass: Set \(\frac{A(t)}{200} = 0.10\): \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/5730} = 0.10 \Rightarrow \frac{t}{5730}\ln(0.5) = \ln(0.10) \Rightarrow t = 5730\frac{\ln(0.10)}{\ln(0.5)} \approx \mathbf{19{,}035\mathrm{\ years}}.\)
